projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Harold Parsons was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: In 1941, I was a college senior in Massachusetts.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where did you go to school in Massachusetts?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: I was going to school, college, in Quincy, Massachusetts. My home was in Melrose, Massachusetts -- suburban Boston.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Well, I have the dubious distinction of being one of the first ones drafted. I was a college senior and I was drafted by the Quincy draft board, and I was a college senior and they said I was drafted. One of the board members came up to me afterwards and said it was unusual to draft a senior in college. The war hadn't begun; this was in the fall of '41. And he said you can appeal. Well, my feeling was I would feel there was something wrong with me if I couldn't make the army, and I said no, I wouldn't appeal. I started college in fall of '41 and in October I was drafted out and I came in through Fort Devons(ph) in Massachusetts. And, again, the U.S. wasn't prepared, and my first duty was to guard the water tower at Fort Devons(ph) with a piece of wood on my shoulder, no rifles. And that's the way it began. Went from Fort Devons(ph) to Fort Lee, Virginia, and December 7, 1941 -- on December 6, we were practicing in the Civil War trenches in Petersburg, Virginia outside of Richmond, Virginia. Pearl Harbor occurred on Sunday. It was their practice to keep one platoon available in case -- we were close to Richmond, Virginia -- some activity come up, they needed extra people. So we were confined to our barracks and couldn't leave the area. Sunday morning, December 7, we were there reading the Richmond paper and one fellow had a radio on, and it said that the Japanese had bombed Pearl Harbor and everybody said, "Where the hell is Pearl Harbor?" That started from the trenches of the Civil War to where we were -- it's interesting -- we were about to have, we were all northerners. New England fellows were on one side of the barracks; the other side the fellows were from Brooklyn, New York, and you needed an interpreter to find out what the fellow from Brooklyn was saying. Of course, we from New England didn't have any accent, so it was quite an interesting thing. We were all complaining about the food. We didn't have enough food, and they told us they would talk to us about it the following week. Well, we never talked about that. When on December 7 Franklin Roosevelt declared war, the following day, we were all lined up on the parade ground and there were loud speakers where we declared war -- we were officially at war. And from there I went -- I was a college student so they thought I had chemical and physical background in studies so they put me in the medical corps. I was inducted into the U.S. Air Force which is Army Air Force at that time. I went from there -- oh, they gave us a pass. I had my first pass was from three days from Virginia to go home since war had started. And I had to be back in camp Christmas Eve. They gave everybody a three-day pass and when we came back I was shipped down south to Keesler Field in Biloxi, Mississippi. Then they split our group up. Half of us went to Biloxi and half of us went to Brookley Field in Mobile, Alabama. I became the head of the hospital laboratory at that air base, Brookley Field. I guess I was there for a year and a half or two years and the war was going on -- oh, they gave us some examinations. As they needed more and more men, they needed more and more officers. So they called us in, the heads of all the departments, gave us an examination afterwards and, apparently, I scored well on it and they called me in and wanted to have me go to officer candidate school. By this time, I went in at 21 dollars a month. I was reading the Plain Dealer the other day and they were talking about what soldiers are receiving today. We went in at 21 dollars a month and we took out a war bond, so much a month, and we had to take out G.I. insurance and I still have my original two thousand dollars worth of G.I. insurance. I still have it today. That was taken out and you took out for laundry. By the time we got through with all that, we had 10 or 11 dollars a month. When I was looking at the Plain Dealer article the other day. I thought how can you pay anybody to go through what these guys are going through today? A baseball player has a minimum, if he is a major leaguer, three hundred thousand, or football, and these guys are putting their lives on the line. I was listening to one of the correspondents saying how they had to wear their suits and gas masks and all this kind of stuff, and it had been three days since they had a shower. Well, I can remember that when we were in Europe we would have a ration of a canteen of water, and your steel helmet was your bathtub. I can remember the first time we got a chance to get a shower, when we were in -- after we landed in France, was -- I wrote a three-page letter talking about a hot shower. Three minutes. But how can you pay men to do this and receive criticism from people who have never given up anything for their country? We were doing it for 21; I think I became a corporal I got 54 dollars. When I was a sergeant I got 78 dollars -- this is a month, this is a month...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything unusual or interesting things happen during your training time?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Let's see. Nothing especially. Our training was cut short, of course, by Pearl Harbor and then we went down to Brookley Field and we were the first ones in the field, and I remember my first experience. That field was brand new, and a light plane had crashed, and my first experience was we had to go out and pick up the body of the pilot in that light plane crash. I was a kid, you're talking about how young you are, you're 19, 20 years old. We had to pick up the body, and I picked up the guy's boot and his leg was still in it. We had to put him on the stretcher and had to take him in; one guy was throwing up. That was my first experience with anything like that. It's something you don't forget.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you attached to a particular outfit at that time?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: I was attached to the station hospital of Brookley Field air base and stayed there for a year, year and a half. I thought I had it made. I was at that time a sergeant and instead of being in the full dormitory of a barracks, I had a private room with another sergeant. That's pretty high living in the military. So, I was very happy being there. After they gave you the examinations, written examinations, and apparently I scored well, they wanted me to go to officer training school, and I didn't go then. I talked my way out of it, and several months later they called me back in and said this time you're going. So I went from Mobile to Texas and went through four months of training and became a 2nd lieutenant. I went back from there to Jackson, Mississippi, the air base at Jackson, Mississippi. I went back to Texas. I went to Fort McPherson, Atlanta, Georgia. I went to Walter Reed in Washington, D.C., and I went back to Mississippi and finally went from Mississippi to an army base outside of Chicago. There we formed into units to go overseas. Went from there, we formed our unit, the 170th General Hospital, and went from there to New York. One interesting thing was we left from New York on a hospital ship heading for Europe, and they made me the interim finance officer and gave me a little safe with a hundred thousand dollars American in it to pay the troops after we landed in France. So you went over to -- my first ocean voyage.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that, late 1943?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Yeah, about '43. Landed in Southampton, England. Just about the time -- we only spent about two,three days in England and then went on an LCI, and we were in the invasion. We didn't get there on D-day but the first week of D-day, after D-day. We came in over Omaha Beach and went up that hill. Then we were in what we call Mudville. I can't remember where it was. Cherbourg was still in the hands of the Germans. The Germans were to the left of us, to the right of us and in back of us. The only thing we had was a small area. Probably, if you remember, the invasion didn't go as well as expected. We were right in the middle. Our first encampment was at Saint-Mere Eglise. That's where the paratroopers came in on D-day, and that's where we set up because it was a strategic spot. They had to go between Cherbourg and the main road; they had to control that and I never knew when Cherbourg fell because I remember after we got there -- I went over as the assistant attachment commander of the troops. We had about 350 G.I.'s in our unit, and I was the assistant CO. I had them out there one time just after we landed along the hedgerows and, I was trying to tell the men this was not a drill -- they had to keep down, this was for real. And a captain was standing there laughing at us, and I said "Captain, you should pay attention to this, too." He was a doctor, big tall fellow. The next day he was sent up to the Cherbourg area and within a week he had been killed. It made you think that -- I remember when we were walking along the hedgerows going from one spot to another that I was on the point, I was leading, and I picked up an American helmet. It had a bullet hole right straight through the center of it. When I picked it up to toss it to one side, the remains was still in the helmet. This gets you aware of the situation you are in right in a hurry. We went across the English Channel on a landing craft, LCI, landing craft infantry. It was a large one, and we landed on Omaha Beach, and I remember walking up that hill. The cemetery is now off to the left of that hill. When I first saw it as we came in -- by this time they had sunk the ships and they built a ramp so they could get vehicles in. We walked up that hill, and when I first saw that I said, "My God, how did anyone live to get up there?" And I couldn't go back to France when they had the 50th anniversary, but I went back a couple of years later and my reaction was the same, how in the world did anybody live to get up the top of the hill and get up where those bunkers were? The military cemetery is there now with over 9,000 and something, just under 10,000 crosses and when I went back there a few years ago, I was very pleased to see how beautiful the cemetery is kept. You know, it isn't what you do; it is where you are. And anybody that got through that was just fortunate, and I was very pleased when we went back to see how well kept the cemetery was, and it was on a weekend and a lot of French people, French children, were there, very reverent. And we went to Saint-Mere Eglise. I was looking -- we had set up in Saint-Mere Eglise because between Cherbourg and there, that was the main area that had to be under control. I went back to Saint-Mere Eglise -- We were stationed there quite some time because the battle for Normandy was not as fast as they thought it would be. It was a long time. They had a shop that had souvenirs of the area and Mary Elaine and I went in and was looking around. She wanted to get some maps and so forth. There was a big French woman there in charge of it, and the woman was trying to help us and Mary Elaine said to the woman that Harold was here during the war, and in spite of what reaction we have gotten from France, the old-timers are different. She threw her arms around me, gave me a big hug and thanked me for being there. Which also makes me think about when VE day was coming in France. Now this was a different part of France from Normandy Beach. We went down, we had our set up was at a rail center in France because at that time there weren't any helicopters or anything. You put the wounded on trains and sent them back via train. The night before VE day was proclaimed, three or four of us got in a jeep and went down to a little town -- little French town -- outside the rail center and we went in -- they have some French bread and wine -- and celebrate the end of the war. We had our jeep parked outside, so we were in there having French bread and wine, and the French people were very friendly and very nice. Finally, we left because we were going to be in the VE day parade the next day, and we come out and that jeep was covered with flowers. The old time French people remember. Some of these new people don't remember, and it is too bad. But I'm glad I had the experience. I wouldn't want to do it again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other stories you remember from the Normandy campaign?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Well, I was a young -- talking about how young the soldiers are -- I was 19, 20. I was in for five years. That's a long time. I was going to be -- ever since I was in the junior high I was going to go to law school. Well, I never got to law school after five years in the military. But I remember being on the trains up close to the front to our base hospital and being strafed by a German plane. You have to remember, at those times they didn't have all the sophistication they had. They made a pass and sprayed us with gunfire but apparently then realized it was a hospital train and pulled off. The bad part about war is you never know if it's a good guy that's really doing his duty or one that's going to take a shot at you no matter what. But we stayed and after the VE day we started to get civilians and everything from the death camps and that was an interesting -- horrible -- experience to see what happened to those people.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How close was your hospital to the front lines usually?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: We were a general hospital so we were further back, quite a ways. You have the evac hospitals, but we would get the serious cases and when people say you don't know what war is like, you have to be in a hospital to see what war is like. It was interesting because we were young and very impressionable. Of course, after the Normandy thing we took a lot of prisoners. I was assistant CO of the attachment, and I became the CO and as an additional duty, I became the head of a thousand German prisoners of war. That was an interesting experience, too. People don't know that we always treated -- we never had the kind of thing you are having in Iraq now where they use hospitals for cover. Ours was just to treat wounded people and there was nothing else. I know, with me, when they said you have a thousand G.I.'s (sic) and there was a lot of things you could do these prisoners around. One of the amusing things was one time we had the German prisoners working at the laundry, and you know there is a lot of laundry at a hospital. They said something was slow in the laundry. So I said to the first sergeant to go down and find out what is making things slow in the laundry. He came back and I said what's holding it up and he said, "You are." And I said, "What do you mean, I am?" He said, "They're ironing your socks." I didn't even know they knew who was in charge.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They just did that for you? Yeah. It used to be irritating. They knew what was going on. It always kinda irritated me they would know everything that was going on. Most Germans realized that if they came into American hands they were lucky, and we had a thousand German POW's there to do all the menial things around the hospital and so forth. When the Battle of the Bulge came, of course, we lost a lot of American soldiers and lost a lot of armaments. They came through -- we had an MP platoon that did the guard work for our thousand German prisoners. They came through and took all of our weapons. Left us with a thousand German POW's and the only thing we had was my carbine and my .45 with a thousand POW's. Like I said, it used to irritate me. They knew what was going on. They knew how the war was going. They were sharp, and when that happened it was an uneasy feeling, one carbine and one .45 with a thousand Germans. But up the road from us about a mile was a French prisoner of war camp. If we had any trouble we said we were going to transfer you to the French. Then we didn't have any more troubles. The French had lost families and so forth and so on, and the French would shoot and ask questions afterwards. The Americans wouldn't do that. So usually we didn't have any trouble. When they came through and did that we asked the French to come down. They came down and brought a machine gun. The Germans were behind barbed wire but they were in pup tents and they were living underground. So we had the French fire over their heads with the machine guns and said, stay there. Well, they did. I was sure glad that French camp was there. It was an interesting experience. You got to come home by points. I had enough points because I was in for five years and I had been overseas for about two years and when the thing came they sent us to Le Havre to process troops going home. And people don't understand that, like the present wars, the mines are a constant danger. I was sent to Le Havre for a good part of our unit to process troops going home. Le Havre, they had cigarette camps, Old Gold, Chesterfield and so forth. Usually your friends are on this hill; you're on this hill. In the evening we would get in a jeep and go across and meet with others going home. One night we had been doing this, oh, half a dozen times. We were taking the road from our camps to the cigarette camp on the other hill and the MP came up and stopped us and we said, "What's the matter?" And he said, "The jeep in front of you just got blown up, hit a mine." We had been over that same road half a dozen times, didn't hit it just right. When we were at Le Havre every morning the sappers would be out locating the mines. Every afternoon for months those mines would be exploded. Just all afternoon, would be exploded. So finally, we are sending troops home from Le Havre. Ships going. Finally, they said your turn is come. You're going home. By this time it was December of after the war was over. So I sent a cable home saying that I am leaving on Saturday, heading home. What I didn't know was I was getting on a ship, all I did was go across the channel to England. Stayed in England. Stayed in a big old English castle, and it was winter. So we would form a semicircle in front of the fireplace, and we would all be sitting in front of the fireplace keeping warm and someone would give a signal and everyone would turn their backs to the fireplace. I stayed there for a month and I came home just, I guess I landed in New York just about Christmas time. Because I know I missed five Christmas's during that war without being home. It was an experience that I'm glad I had, but I wouldn't want to do it again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was your hospital in France then the whole time you were there? You didn't move up?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Yeah. We moved a number of places in France but we were always in France because we were the biggest unit of hospitals, so they always located near good rail facilities. They had to go through evac hospitals and emergency hospitals, and then the serious cases had to get up to the general hospital, and after the general hospital they would go home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you treat a lot of casualties during the Bulge then?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I thought we were going to lose it all then. That's interesting because by that time we had pretty well -- we had Quonset huts for the officers and so forth, and you always lived in a tent. I lived in a tent for so long I have never gotten in a tent since the war. I won't go in a tent. As I say, I had a thousand German POWs and they had a lot of talents with them. So we had an artist from Leipzig, Germany, and he could make good charcoal drawings and so forth. So I thought well, we could dress up our mess halls and so forth. Everyone wanted to get them so I had them stuck in one part of my office complex so he couldn't be subverted by somebody else. I had him dress up our -- huge pictures, I have an album in here I think that shows it -- one of the things I was really lucky, my tent mate all the time we were overseas was McEvoy(ph) and he had been to Europe twice before the war. So after the war was over, we got a chance to travel a little bit around France and that was -- he was like a big brother to me. He was 10 years older than I was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was he your best buddy over there?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would you do for fun if you had a break during the war?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: We had a chance to go back to England on furlough. He was going to Ireland because Maureen O'Hara, the actress, was a friend of his and he said, "Harold, I asked her and she said to bring you along." Well, I had spent so little time in England I wanted to spend more time in England so I didn't go.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You passed up a chance to meet Maureen O'Hara?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, boy. So what was it like in England? How were the English people towards Americans?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Oh, fine. I had a great time. I'll always remember seeing Piccadilly Circus and they sang "When the Lights Go On Again." At that time the war was still on and the buzz bombs were coming over.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The first time you were there only a few days before you went over in the invasion? Is that right?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you must have crossed over in May or June of '44?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: The best I can make out, we landed on Omaha Beach in first week of June 6th. So some time between June 6th and June 15th, I was in there. Because Cherbourg was still in German hands, and when I went back I found out that Cherbourg fell. I forget the exact date on it, but I know from that it had to be in the first week that we landed. Of course, when we landed there we weren't thinking about that. We were just hoping we could get home again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get any USO shows or anything like that in France?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Yeah. In fact, I was the morale officer so I had to deal with the USO troops.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any big names come?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: No. None of the big names came to us. I used to get mostly French. Here's one of the pictures he did in our mess hall. After the war was over we received a prize, one of the finest enlisted men's mess halls. All of these things taken from The Stars and Stripes and that kind of thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: As far as the concentration camp survivors you treated, were they French citizens that were coming back to France?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Yeah. I remember going down and seeing one of the first ones that came in and, oh boy, not good. Here's what I was trying to find for you. These are all pictures of the mess hall. Those are scenes from The Stars and Stripes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sad Sack. Is that Sad Sack?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Yeah, that's Sad Sack.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So these paintings were hanging from the ceiling like?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And a lovely lady with 2 G.I.s; so he took things from Yank Magazine?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: I would pick them out, and he would work them. I will show you here he did one for me that hung in my office of Eisenhower.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. That is great.

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: He did this at my request, and one of the others made a frame. It's interesting, no matter where you are, if you go like this it looks like his eyes are following you. No matter where you are sitting in the room you think he is looking directly at you. That was in the office, and when I came to come home I carried that and it stuck out. "Boy, you are crazy trying to get that thing home in one piece." Well, I got it home in one piece. This thing was in the center window of _____. They must have had it for two or three weeks. END OF FIRST SECTION OF CD, PORTION SR0001001; START OF SECOND SECTION OF CD, PORTION SR0002002. And it's interesting. One of the kids I had in school was living in Texas and apparently got the Painesville Telegraph sent to them and she sent me a letter and said -- had a picture, this picture -- in the paper and said who it came from and so forth. I got a letter from her saying she was a student of mine after I came out from the war, so it's surprising how things got around.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever get a chance to meet Eisenhower?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: No, I never saw Eisenhower.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Or Patton or any of the generals?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: No, never saw any of the big ones. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember mail call, getting letters, packages from home?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Yes. I married my college sweetheart, and I would have been a senior. She was a junior, and when I went into the service she decided she was going to get through school as fast as she could. So she actually did three years of college and a summer school and graduated. Of course, this is during the war, and she came home to Ohio and started teaching, never had student teaching, and she taught for 28 years and had student teachers all the time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: She sent you a lot of letters and things like that?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: She sent me V-mail every day. And she sent us care packages. It was interesting. I had to tell her -- she was doing chocolates and all those kinds of things. By that time we could get the PXs and I could get them there. She was doing without and sending them in there, and Jay, who was my tent mate all this time, and he and I still get together. He's 10 years older than I am. We get together about every two years. In fact, last fall -- he lives in San Francisco so we were going to take a ship from San Francisco up to Alaska and went out and he had a stroke the night before we were to go. He ended up in the hospital; so we just had that one night with him. But we were doing it so we could have the 10 days or 12 days on the cruise. We get together about every couple of years. Sometimes he would go out here. He was in the equity business, and he had foreign accounts in Australia and Europe and so forth, and he would stop off on his way to and from, and I went out one year and we spent a week down at Monterey Peninsula. Just the two of us. He would do the cooking and I would do the washing. Real great. We still keep in touch. He's okay, but he's 93 so he's not doing too much.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you finally got home in 1945, what was that reunion with your wife like?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Oh, I'm telling you, it was great. She was teaching school in Ashtabula county. I got to New York; I thought things had worked out. I was coming into New York, and I thought she would get up there, and there was some kind of mix up and when I got home to Boston I said where's Goldie (ph), and they said she's in Ohio. I got on the phone and, boy, she got the next train out. It's interesting. She was coming in on the train so I went into South Station to meet her train, and she was coming up and I was waiting at the station. She had been sitting with some man. She came running and he said, "Give me your suitcases and I'll..." We had a great reunion. She died 1987. Cancer. Mary Elaine -- who gave you the call -- her husband was a purple hearter in the Battle of the Bulge,and he died of cancer. So I was real lucky. I had a great 44 years with my wife, and then to meet Mary Elaine, and she had gone through all these things the same way. So I think I've been very fortunate. Came through without a scratch.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences over there, does any other particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Oh, one of the most interesting things was that Jay, my roommate, he had been to Europe a couple of times. He had some friends in San Francisco who were French. When we were at Le Mans, the rail center, these people had a chateau -- I probably have a picture of it here somewhere -- anyway, they used to, they had this big chateau close, oh, within 10 miles of our hospital set up, so they had -- every Thursday night they would have us come out to eat with them. Being young and healthy, we would eat at the officer's mess and I had a jeep assigned to me. He and I would get on it and we would drive over to the chateau. And this was one of those -- we have many courses. Every Thursday night we would go over and eat with them, and the men would retire to one room and have cigars and cognac and so forth, and the women would go out some place, another room. This was kinda nice. The war was winding down. The fighting was up in Germany and we were in France, and we had this every Friday (sic) night, so one Friday night we were going, and we said we won't be here next Thursday night and they said why not. Remember, we are living out in the middle of the woods. We were in a tent with a black pot belly stove, in the mud -- oh, and when we were in Mudville the mud was so deep the six by six's, the big trucks, we would have to take the steel chain on it, attach it around a tree and winch the truck through the mud. That's how big the mud was. This was a little better when we were up there. I can show you some of the photographs up here and we used to have a big mirror and some of the guys, we would say, "Remember Mudville. Look nice". So we told them we can't be here next Thursday night. And they said, "Why not?" and we said, "We have a leave to Paris. We have three nights in Paris." And they said, "where are you going to stay?" We said the army set up hotels where you stay when you are on leave. And they said, "oh, you can't do that." And we said, "Why not?" "Well, we have an apartment overlooking the Eiffel Tower and the Seine River, and you are going to stay there." We said, "That's wonderful". Here we leave the mud and the pot belly stove, we go to this apartment overlooking the Eiffel Tower and have a butler and a maid to take care of us. If that wasn't a contrast -- that was a contrast. That was nice. This same family -- I have a book over there they sent me -- they had two daughters and the daughters were in Ireland when the war broke out, and they didn't know how their parents were making out, and the parents didn't know how the daughters were making out. Anyway, they got home before we broke up and went home. So we got to meet them, and they wrote a book telling their experiences which came as a surprise to me. I thought they were living the life of Riley. Well, they weren't. It was the opposite. The girl wrote a book with some pictures and so forth in it and sent a copy to Jay and one to me. A couple of years ago I had a niece going to Kirkland(ph) High School, and they wanted someone to tell them a little about War World II, and I took up that book to tell them because she was that age, and I said how lucky they were compared to these girls.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They were living in Ireland at that time?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: They were in Ireland until the end of the war. But it makes you grow up in a hurry, and the fellows that survive this, it will be something they will never forget, and it will make them better people for their experience.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Let's see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: I think so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Think you got it? I don't have a lot of specific questions because I don't know what you went through specifically, so if anything comes to mind?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Well, it sure made me grow up in a hurry. As I say, I'm glad I had the experience, but I wouldn't want to do it again. In fact, my roommate, when I was talking to him on the phone I said, "Jay, let's you and I sit this one out."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were the Germans pretty good about respecting the medical corps if they knew it was a hospital or medical...

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: I think they were. That one time with the strafing I'm sure was an accident. We never had anything that you would consider anything wrong. And I only had one trouble with a German prisoner. He was a real fanatic. The sergeant had me come down because he had given him so much trouble. I was sitting in back of a desk, with a soldier with a rifle and bayonet, and I had a .45 and he was in the front of the desk, like where you are, and I thought he was going to come over the desk and try to throttle me. He was a real -- that's the only one I can ever remember. I had two prisoners escape and I thought they were crazy. They were not going to have it any easier than under us. We made sure they got everything they were entitled to and, and they were treated kindly. We didn't pamper them. We made sure they were well taken care of because we wanted our prisoners treated the same way and, hopefully, they were. That's what motivated us was we wanted them to be treated the same way we wanted our prisoners to be treated.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that guy with the SS?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: Yeah. And it just amazed me, here he was in the middle of France with a good situation and they knew the French were up the road but as I said, two of them did escape and I thought that's crazy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You never heard about what happened to those two?

sp.speaker: Harold Parsons
sp.p: No. And no one would ever tell you because if someone escapes they would never put them back in the same prison because they want to know what's on the outside, and you don't want them to know that. But I don't know what happened to them, and it was so close to the end of the war that it was ridiculous. But, as you can see, we had some real nice people. They were happy -- most of them were just delighted to be in American hands. Let's see. Can't think of anything right now. I hope I didn't waste your time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not at all. END OF FINAL SECTION OF CD, PORTION SR001002.
